results.content: # Usage of the verb "provide". Does the verb "provide" always have to be used with "with"? > Can you provide me *with* some good examples? > Can you provide me some good examples? > Can you provide some good examples? If you could give me some good examples regarding "provide" with different types of usage, I'd appreciate that. The verb *provide* takes two objects, and they can go in either order. > Can you provide some good examples **for** me. >  Can you provide me **with** some good examples. Provide can be either transitive or intransitive. >  • present or yield (something useful) : *neither will provide answers to these problems.*. @Cerberus: I just found a Wikipedia page that says "Can you provide me some good examples" is grammatical in American but not British English. Other uses of *provide* could be:. >  I can provide for you. >  Can you provide an answer? 0") "provided me" or "provided to me". 20") Preposition with verb "provide".

results.content: >    Don't say, for example 'The animals provide food to their young'. > This provides food for thought. * The will provided for their upkeep. ldoceonline.com/dictionary/provide GRAMMAR: Patterns with provide • You provide something for someone: We provide information for parents. • You provide someone with something: We provide parents with information. ✗Don’t say: We provide parents information. * We provide information for parents. I mean according to your explanation, 'We provide information to parents' should be correct, shouldn't it? Provide certainly has a meaning of "hand over" or "give to," so I can't see how it can be ungrammatical to use a "to" preposition in phrases using "provide.". You can also "provide an answer to a question." You certainly can "provide a shoulder to cry on." In either case, using "for" instead of "to" wouldn't make sense. You can say "provide a shoulder for her to cry on," however. * I agree with comment and answers that say you can "provide something to someone.".

results.title: word choice - "provide" vs. "provide with" - English Language & Usage ...
results.content: > We add the information their study provides with to our article. Usage of the verb "provide". In the first, the material provided is the object, in the second the recipient is the object. > We add the information the study provides us with to our article. > We add the information the study provides to our article. In AmE, you can indeed say *"We add the information the study provides us to our article."* See Wikipedia and this ELU.SE question. Indeed, it would be simpler (and clearer) to say "We add the information *provided by* the study to our article". > We add the information the study provides *us* with to our article. In your original sentence, the prepositional phrase "with information" didn't modify any words. In your example *with information* doesn't modify *us* (in the way it would in *They saw us with the information*); rather, it specifies part of the activity of providing. 16") Usage of the verb "provide".
